paragraphs: Predicting a vehicle’s future movement requires accounting for differences in how people drive. The paper argues that methods centered on motion history and interactions with the environment do not adequately capture this source of variation. Its Driving-Style-Adaptive framework, DSA, incorporates driving styles directly into trajectory prediction, making behavioral differences part of how the prediction is constructed.

DSA represents trajectory patterns using sets of basis functions tailored to different driving styles. These functions provide building blocks for approximating a vehicle’s movement. The framework dynamically combines them and adjusts their degree, allowing the resulting representation to adapt to different trajectory patterns. This construction also provides explanatory information about the prediction process through the functions used to represent a trajectory.

Experiments on public datasets containing real-world driving show that DSA outperforms the state-of-the-art methods evaluated. The stated contribution is therefore both predictive and explanatory: explicitly representing driving-style variation improves the reported predictions while giving insight into how those predictions are formed.
neurips-2025-a-driving-style-adaptive-fr.tldr: DSA represents different driving styles with adaptable trajectory functions, improving prediction accuracy and providing insight into its predictions.

paragraphs: SignViP generates sign language videos from spoken-language text while aiming to preserve the signer’s identity. Existing approaches often connect text translation to video generation through a single coarse representation, such as a skeleton sequence. The paper instead uses detailed poses and three-dimensional hand information to provide richer guidance for natural and expressive signing.

The framework learns this guidance in stages. A video diffusion model and a multi-condition encoder first learn continuous representations of motion and appearance. An autoencoder then compresses these representations and converts them into discrete tokens using finite scalar quantization. A separate translator learns to predict those tokens from text. This makes the translation target compact rather than requiring direct prediction of high-dimensional conditions.

At generation time, the predicted tokens are decoded into continuous representations that guide the video diffusion model. Reported experiments show state-of-the-art performance across video quality, temporal coherence, and semantic fidelity. These findings support the proposed combination of detailed motion guidance and compact tokenization for producing videos that remain coherent over time and faithful to the intended signing content.
neurips-2025-advanced-sign-language-vide.tldr: SignViP translates text into compact tokens encoding detailed pose and hand information to guide higher-quality sign language video generation.

paragraphs: Chain-of-Model learning organizes a model so that it can grow progressively and operate at several sizes. Its central idea is to divide each layer’s hidden representation into multiple components called chains. Information access follows an ordered dependency: an output chain can use preceding input chains, giving the representation a structure that supports different chain counts.

The authors apply this design to Transformer layers in Chain-of-Language-Model, or CoLM. Additional chains can expand a model built from earlier chains, while selecting fewer or more chains provides differently sized submodels for inference. CoLM-Air adds a sharing mechanism: keys and values are computed within the first chain and reused across the others. The abstract identifies model switching and faster prefilling as additional capabilities enabled by this design.

Experiments show that the CoLM family achieves performance comparable to a standard Transformer while offering progressive scaling and flexible inference sizes. The contribution is an architectural way to connect model growth during training with deployment flexibility, allowing multiple operating sizes within the same chain-based framework.
neurips-2025-chain-of-model-learning-for.tldr: CoLM structures Transformer representations into ordered chains, enabling progressive model growth and multiple inference sizes with comparable reported performance.

paragraphs: Compressing labelled data requires deciding which statistical relationships the smaller dataset should preserve. This paper targets conditional distributions directly, addressing a gap in methods originally developed for unlabelled data. It introduces Average Maximum Conditional Mean Discrepancy, or AMCMD, to compare conditional distributions, together with a closed-form estimator.

The authors show that, for their compression setting, the construction cost associated with targeting this metric can fall from cubic to linear in the number of data points. They use this result to develop Average Conditional Kernel Herding, a greedy selection algorithm. They also introduce Joint Kernel Herding to study compression of the joint distribution, making the choice between joint and conditional preservation an explicit comparison.

Two further methods optimize the compressed set collectively instead of selecting it through a greedy heuristic, while retaining linear complexity. Experiments favor the conditional version, ACKIP, over both joint-distribution compression and greedy conditional selection. The joint optimization method JKIP also consistently outperforms its greedy counterpart. These results support both directly targeting conditional structure and improving how the compressed set is optimized.
neurips-2025-conditional-distribution-co.tldr: The paper develops linear-complexity methods for compressing labelled data, with experiments favoring direct conditional-distribution preservation and collective optimization.

paragraphs: The paper approaches robotic grasp generation by transferring high-quality grasps from shape templates to new objects within the same category. This targets a tension between stable but inefficient analytical approaches and generative methods whose generalization is constrained by available data. The proposed framework uses object similarity and task requirements to guide that transfer.

Instead of transferring a hand configuration directly, the method generates an object contact map with a conditional diffusion model. A dual mapping mechanism captures geometric relationships between the template and the new object. Two additional representations, a part map and a direction map, describe finer contact details. A cascade of conditional diffusion models transfers the three maps together while maintaining their consistency.

A final recovery stage selects reliable contact points and optimizes the grasp configuration. Experiments report a favorable balance among grasp quality, generation efficiency, and generalization across tasks. The same-category transfer setting is central to the approach: its stated mechanism adapts template knowledge to new shapes through coordinated contact representations.
neurips-2025-contact-map-transfer-with-c.tldr: A conditional diffusion framework transfers coordinated contact maps from templates to new objects within the same category to generate dexterous grasps.

paragraphs: A multi-bit quantization network supports several numerical precision levels within one model, providing flexibility at deployment. Training can be expensive because existing approaches repeatedly update each precision variant on the full dataset. Supporting additional or intermediate precisions can also require further fine-tuning. This paper addresses both sources of training overhead.

Its first technique corrects weight bias introduced by quantization. By aligning activation distributions across bit-widths, the method enables shared batch normalization and removes the need for the extra fine-tuning stage described in the abstract. The second technique assigns each precision variant a compact, informative training subset. These subsets are selected using gradient-based importance scores, taking advantage of implicit knowledge transfer among the variants.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-1K with ResNet and Vision Transformer architectures. The method achieves competitive or better accuracy while delivering training speedups of up to 7.88 times. The findings indicate that repeated full-dataset training can be substantially reduced in the evaluated settings by combining precision alignment with selective use of training examples.
neurips-2025-efficient-multi-bit-quantiz.tldr: Weight bias correction and precision-specific data subsets reduce multi-bit network training costs, with reported speedups of up to 7.88 times.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous Adversarial Play, or HAP, develops an automatic curriculum through interaction between a teacher and a learner. The paper argues that conventional self-play, built around symmetric competitors, is poorly matched to open-ended settings with different instructional and problem-solving roles. Its motivating question is how an artificial teacher can construct suitable challenges without a predefined hierarchy of tasks.

HAP models the teacher and learner as participants in a minimax optimization process. The teacher generates tasks, the learner attempts to solve them, and their adversarial interaction changes both over time. A bidirectional feedback mechanism lets the teacher continually adjust task complexity using the learner’s current performance. The curriculum therefore responds to the learner’s development during training.

Experiments across multi-task learning domains show performance on par with state-of-the-art baselines. The generated curricula also improve learning efficacy in the reported studies involving artificial agents and human participants. These findings support adaptive teacher–learner interaction as a way to construct useful curricula while maintaining competitive task performance.
neurips-2025-heterogeneous-adversarial-p.tldr: HAP co-trains a task-generating teacher and a problem-solving learner to produce adaptive curricula with competitive reported performance.

paragraphs: Jasmine adapts Stable Diffusion’s learned visual knowledge to self-supervised depth estimation from a single image. The difficulty is that reprojection-based training can introduce blur and artifacts when images contain occlusion, little texture, or changing illumination. Those imperfect training signals can undermine the detailed visual information that makes the pretrained diffusion model useful.

The framework introduces a mix-batch image reconstruction task that reconstructs images themselves without additional supervision. This auxiliary task preserves the model’s detail priors while protecting depth estimation from degradation. Jasmine also adds a Scale-Shift GRU to reconcile two different estimation behaviors: Stable Diffusion’s scale-and-shift invariance and the scale invariance of the self-supervised depth setting. The module additionally shields fine-grained output texture from interference by the reprojection loss.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on KITTI and superior zero-shot generalization across multiple datasets. The results support adapting a diffusion model’s visual priors through carefully designed self-supervised objectives, rather than relying on the high-precision supervision used by the earlier Stable Diffusion depth methods described in the abstract.
neurips-2025-jasmine-harnessing-diffusio.tldr: Jasmine combines image reconstruction and scale-shift adaptation to use Stable Diffusion’s visual priors for self-supervised depth estimation.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning agents can lose neuronal activity, reducing their ability to adapt as new data arrives. A common diagnostic uses neuron activations to estimate how much expressive capacity remains. The paper argues that this diagnostic becomes less statistically informative in more complex architectures, even though it works well for simpler multilayer perceptron agents.

The authors shift attention to a neuron’s capacity to learn through gradient updates. Their Gradient Magnitude Neural Activity Metric, GraMa, uses gradients to quantify that capacity at the neuron level. It is designed to be lightweight and independent of a particular architecture. The reported analysis shows that it exposes persistent inactivity in residual networks, diffusion models, and agents using different activation functions.

The paper also introduces ReGraMa, which resets neurons according to the GraMa measurement. This intervention consistently improves learning across the evaluated reinforcement learning algorithms and benchmarks, including MuJoCo and the DeepMind Control Suite. The findings connect a different diagnostic signal with a practical intervention for improving adaptation during learning.
neurips-2025-measure-gradients-not-activ.tldr: GraMa measures neuron learning capacity through gradients, and using it to guide neuron resets improves performance across the tested reinforcement learning settings.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates mathematical reasoning as a complete pipeline: read a natural-language problem, translate it into Lean, and produce a proof that corresponds to the original problem. That final correspondence matters because successfully proving a formal statement does not establish that the system solved the intended informal question.

The authors find that the pipeline can achieve only about 36% accuracy using state-of-the-art models from the literature, despite separately reported autoformalization and proving accuracies of 97% and 69%. Their analysis identifies discrepancies between formal and informal statements in more than half of miniF2F’s problems as a substantial contributor to the drop. They correct errors, discrepancies, and simplifications to create miniF2F-v2 with verified statements and proofs.

In the reported comparison of full theorem-proving pipelines, the best accuracy reaches 70% on the revised benchmark versus 40% on the original. The authors still find substantial misalignment between translation models and theorem provers. Their results show why benchmark statement quality and end-to-end evaluation both matter for understanding progress in formal mathematical reasoning.
neurips-2025-minif2f-lean-revisited-revi.tldr: The authors repair widespread statement discrepancies in miniF2F and show how benchmark quality affects end-to-end mathematical reasoning evaluation.

paragraphs: OASIS addresses collaborative graph learning when communication is limited to a single round. This setting is attractive for resource-constrained participants, but the paper argues that existing generative approaches to one-shot federated learning do not adequately capture graph structure. Methods developed primarily for images can miss the detailed relationships that a global graph model needs to learn from local clients.

The framework introduces a Synergy Graph Synthesizer to produce informative synthetic graphs and a Topological Codebook to represent structural information in a latent space. Two Wasserstein-based distillation components then transfer knowledge. One captures relationships between classes, while the other transfers structural relationships represented by the codebook. Together, they address semantic information and graph topology within the same integration process.

Experiments on real-world tasks report superior performance and generalization. The contribution is a graph-specific approach to combining client knowledge under a one-round communication constraint. Its design treats the transfer of structural detail as a central requirement for building the global model.
neurips-2025-oasis-one-shot-federated-gr.tldr: OASIS combines synthetic graphs, a structural codebook, and Wasserstein-based distillation for federated graph learning with one communication round.

paragraphs: This paper studies policy-gradient methods for reinforcement learning objectives beyond standard expected reward. Its setting uses a general concave utility of the state-action occupancy measure, which describes how a policy distributes its visits across states and actions. Such a framework can express problems including imitation learning, exploration, and safe reinforcement learning.

For tabular problems, the authors establish global optimality guarantees using a proof technique based on gradient domination. The technique builds on theoretical developments for standard reinforcement learning and opens possibilities for studying policy representations beyond direct parameterization. The concavity condition on the utility is part of the stated setting of these guarantees.

The analysis also covers large state-action spaces. Here, the method estimates occupancy measures within a chosen function approximation class using maximum likelihood estimation. Its sample complexity depends on the dimension induced by that class instead of the number of state-action pairs. This result makes the complexity of the representation central to the learning guarantee, extending the analysis beyond settings where every state-action pair is explicitly represented.
neurips-2025-on-the-global-optimality-of.tldr: The paper proves global optimality results for policy gradients with concave occupancy-based utilities, including large-space methods whose sample complexity depends on representation dimension.

paragraphs: Conditional diffusion models often need substantial training data, making training from scratch difficult when a new task has few examples. This paper investigates why transferring knowledge from other tasks can reduce that data requirement. Its focus is theoretical sample efficiency: how learning a reusable representation affects the amount of target-task data needed.

The analysis assumes that the conditions across all tasks share a low-dimensional representation. Under that assumption, source tasks can provide a useful representation before learning the target task. The authors show that a well-learned source representation can substantially reduce the target task’s sample complexity. Both the shared structure and the quality of the learned representation are central to the result.

Numerical experiments are included to verify the theoretical findings. The contribution is an initial explanation of conditional diffusion transfer through representation learning: source-task training can supply compact conditional structure that makes subsequent learning more data-efficient. The stated conclusion concerns tasks satisfying that shared-representation setting, with a sufficiently well-learned representation available for transfer.
neurips-2025-provable-sample-efficient-t.tldr: A well-learned shared low-dimensional condition representation can substantially reduce the target-task data needed for conditional diffusion learning.

paragraphs: RealMath evaluates language models on mathematical tasks drawn from research papers and mathematical forums. The authors argue that competition questions, formal proofs, and deliberately difficult problems do not fully represent the mathematics encountered in research work. Their benchmark changes the source of evaluation tasks to better reflect that setting.

The design addresses three practical requirements. It draws on diverse research-level material, uses verifiable statements to support reliable automated assessment, and allows the dataset to be refreshed continually. Refreshability is intended to mitigate contamination risks, helping the evaluation remain useful as models and their training material change. These requirements connect the authenticity of the tasks with the practicality of maintaining and scoring the benchmark.

Experiments across multiple language models reveal unexpectedly strong abilities on research mathematics relative to competition problems. The authors interpret this as evidence that current models may already assist working mathematicians, while acknowledging limitations on highly challenging problems. The result supports evaluating research usefulness directly rather than inferring it entirely from performance on other mathematical benchmarks.
neurips-2025-realmath-a-continuous-bench.tldr: RealMath uses refreshable, verifiable tasks from research papers and forums to assess language models’ potential usefulness in mathematical research.

paragraphs: This paper studies why reasoning through continuous vectors can be efficient for directed graph reachability: deciding whether one vertex can be reached from another. The authors construct a two-layer Transformer that solves the problem using D continuous reasoning steps, where D is the graph diameter. They compare this with the best known constant-depth discrete-reasoning result, which uses O(n²) decoding steps for n vertices.

In their construction, a continuous thought vector represents several search frontiers at once. This superposition supports parallel breadth-first search, allowing the representation to carry multiple possible directions of exploration. The paper contrasts this with discrete reasoning that selects a single path from the represented possibilities and proceeds sequentially. The comparison concerns the stated constructions and known results, rather than establishing a universal lower bound for discrete reasoning.

Experiments examine whether trained models develop behavior consistent with the theory. The authors report that representations of multiple search frontiers emerge without explicit supervision to explore several paths simultaneously. This connects the theoretical mechanism to observed learning dynamics on the studied reasoning problem.
neurips-2025-reasoning-by-superposition-.tldr: A theoretical construction and supporting experiments show how continuous thought vectors can represent parallel graph searches and solve reachability efficiently.

paragraphs: REMI proposes a theory of how grid cells and place cells could jointly support navigation toward a remembered goal. Grid cells represent space through repeating patterns, while place cells respond to particular locations and contextual cues. The paper asks how their interaction might connect cue-triggered recall, internal route planning, and reconstruction of experiences along a planned route.

The proposed mechanism associates sensory inputs with grid-cell patterns through place cells. A sensory cue can then retrieve the grid pattern for a goal location. The authors analytically show that grid-based planning permits shortcuts through unvisited locations and extends local transitions into long-range paths. Intermediate grid states activate place-cell pattern completion, reconstructing sensory experiences as planning proceeds.

A single-layer recurrent neural network models the hippocampal–entorhinal loop together with a planning subnetwork. Simulations in RatatouGym and visually realistic tasks in Habitat Sim demonstrate the proposed effects. The work presents a system-level account of how these representations could cooperate, supported by analysis and navigation simulations.
neurips-2025-remi-reconstructing-episodi.tldr: REMI models how interacting grid and place cells could retrieve remembered goals, plan routes, and reconstruct sensory experiences along them.

paragraphs: Federated continual learning aims to let devices learn from changing data streams while retaining earlier knowledge and preserving data privacy. The paper argues that much existing work emphasizes privacy and restrictions on access to past data without adequately constraining training overhead. For edge devices, storage, computation, and the availability of labels are also central practical limits.

The authors build a large-scale benchmark to evaluate leading methods under different resource budgets. Their experiments include six datasets, typical federated continual learning techniques, and both class-incremental and domain-incremental scenarios. The evaluation uses more than 1,000 GPU hours and includes sensitivity analysis to examine whether the conclusions persist across the tested settings.

Every evaluated approach falls short of expected performance under the limited-resource conditions studied, and the sensitivity analysis supports that finding. The authors interpret the results as evidence that most existing methods depend too heavily on resources for practical deployment. The benchmark makes resource budgets an explicit part of judging continual-learning performance and informs the paper’s discussion of future research directions.
neurips-2025-resource-constrained-federa.tldr: A resource-constrained benchmark finds that all evaluated federated continual learning methods fall short of expected performance under the tested tight budgets.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether deployed AI agents follow their policies when people deliberately try to make them violate those policies. The authors organized a month-long public red-teaming competition involving agents powered by 22 frontier language models. The challenge collected 1.8 million prompt-injection attacks and documented more than 60,000 successful policy violations.

Using this collection, the authors construct a demanding benchmark for evaluating agent security. They report attack success rates near 100% across the agents and associated policies tested on that benchmark. This result concerns the benchmark assembled from the competition data; it is distinct from the proportion of successful attacks among all competition submissions. Their analysis also finds that successful attacks often transfer and apply broadly across tested settings.

The study observes little correlation between robustness and model capability, model size, or inference compute budget. Within this evaluation, those attributes therefore provide limited guidance about resistance to attacks. The benchmark and analysis expose substantial deployment-policy vulnerabilities and provide evidence for the need to improve agent defenses.
neurips-2025-security-challenges-in-ai-a.tldr: A large public attack competition exposes widespread agent policy violations and yields a benchmark with near-total attack success across the tested agents and policies.

paragraphs: Autoregressive text-to-image models generate images through sequential token prediction, which can require thousands of model evaluations. Speculative Jacobi-Denoising Decoding, or SJD2, aims to reduce that work by generating multiple tokens in parallel. It combines iterative Jacobi decoding with a denoising process that helps stabilize the sequence of predictions.

The method first applies low-cost fine-tuning so a pretrained model can accept noisy token embeddings and predict the next clean tokens. At inference, it initializes token sequences with Gaussian noise and repeatedly updates them in embedding space. A probabilistic verification rule decides which proposed tokens can be accepted together. Tokens that are not accepted are refined along the denoising trajectory for another iteration.

Experiments show that SJD2 can reduce the number of forward passes and accelerate generation while maintaining image quality. The contribution is a coordinated adaptation of training and decoding: the model learns to work with noisy intermediate representations, and the inference procedure uses that ability to make and refine parallel token proposals.
neurips-2025-speculative-jacobi-denoisin.tldr: SJD2 combines denoising fine-tuning with parallel speculative decoding to reduce autoregressive image-generation passes while preserving reported visual quality.

paragraphs: Adaptive data analysis lets an analyst choose later questions using answers to earlier ones. Most theory assumes independent data samples, but correlations can make accurate analysis difficult even when questions are fixed in advance. The concentrated-query framework addresses this by restricting attention to queries whose values stay close to their expectations.

That restriction makes the non-adaptive problem straightforward, yet adaptive querying remains harder. Previously known methods in this framework support at most O(n) queries from n samples, compared with O(n²) in the independent setting. The paper asks whether this difference reflects inadequate algorithms or a genuine constraint imposed by the framework.

The authors prove that the gap is inherent under the current concentrated-query formulation, assuming certain natural conditions on the algorithm. They also present a simpler version of the best known algorithms that matches the impossibility result. Together, the lower and upper bounds identify what is achievable within the stated setting, explaining why concentration alone does not recover the adaptive-query capacity associated with independent samples.
neurips-2025-tight-bounds-for-answering-.tldr: Under stated algorithmic conditions, the paper proves that concentrated queries retain an inherent adaptive-query gap from the independent-data setting.

paragraphs: ToF-IP estimates full-body three-dimensional pose by combining sparse inertial sensors with Time-of-Flight distance sensors. Inertial tracking can accumulate errors when it derives position by integrating acceleration over time. Direct distance measurements provide another source of spatial information that mitigates this accumulation. The added sensors increase hardware volume by a reported 3%.

The software combines measurements using a Transformer that treats each sensing node as a token. This explicitly models relationships both within a node’s measurements and between nodes. A dynamic positional encoding also represents the changing spatial positions of wearable nodes through motion-conditioned functions, helping the model capture body dynamics as the wearer moves.

The authors contribute a 208-minute dataset from 10 participants, pairing synchronized inertial and distance measurements with optical tracking ground truth. Experiments report better accuracy than state-of-the-art approaches including PNP, with improvements on complex and slow movements such as Tai Chi. The findings support supplementing portable inertial tracking with direct distance information and a model designed to integrate the two sensor types.
neurips-2025-tof-ip-time-of-flight-enhan.tldr: ToF-IP adds direct distance sensing and tailored sensor integration to improve sparse-inertial full-body motion tracking.

paragraphs: TRACE learns representations of neural time series by using the repeated-trial structure common in neuroscience recordings. Such datasets can contain responses from hundreds or thousands of neurons. Existing contrastive approaches often create training pairs through generic data transformations, leaving the information provided by repeated trials underused.

The method creates positive pairs by averaging different subsets of trials. These paired averages give the contrastive learning process two related representations constructed from the data’s own trial structure. TRACE combines this approach with ideas from neighbor embeddings to learn a two-dimensional representation directly. The resulting embedding provides a compact space for examining similarities and differences in neural responses.

On simulated data, TRACE outperforms comparison methods in resolving fine response differences. In recordings from living animals, its representations capture both continuous biological variation and clusters associated with cell types. They can also assist data quality control. These findings show that exploiting repeated trials can support a representation that retains several distinct forms of biologically relevant structure.
neurips-2025-trace-contrastive-learning-.tldr: TRACE uses averages from different trial subsets to learn two-dimensional neural representations that capture fine response differences and biological structure.

paragraphs: Privileged learning trains a policy with access to informative observations, then derives a deployment policy that must act using partial observations. The two can behave differently because the deployed policy lacks information available during privileged training. Simply penalizing that behavioral gap is difficult when the privileged policy cannot see how much information its counterpart has gathered.

Uncertainty-Sensitive Privileged Learning estimates this information-gathering progress through uncertainty in reconstructing privileged observations from partial ones. It supplies the uncertainty estimate to the privileged policy. Reward transformation and blurring of privileged observations then encourage actions that reduce uncertainty, guiding the policy toward gathering information needed for successful behavior under the deployment observation constraints.

Across nine tasks, the authors report significantly smaller behavioral discrepancies and better deployment performance than the evaluated baselines. Visualizations show the deployment policy quantifying its uncertainty and the privileged policy responding to changes in it. The results support making the learner’s information state visible during privileged training so that training behavior better reflects what deployment can achieve.
neurips-2025-uncertainty-sensitive-privi.tldr: USPL exposes deployment uncertainty to a privileged training policy, encouraging information gathering and reducing the reported training-to-deployment behavior gap.

paragraphs: CurDKV compresses the key-value cache used during autoregressive language-model generation. Many existing methods decide which cached tokens to retain using query-key attention scores. The paper argues that these scores alone overlook value vectors, which directly contribute to the attention output and therefore affect the model’s predictions.

The proposed method uses leverage scores from an approximated CUR matrix decomposition to select keys and values. Its target is the dominant subspace of the attention output, including the contribution of values. The theoretical analysis shows that accurately approximating attention scores does not guarantee preservation of the output, and that CUR-based selection minimizes the stated end-to-end attention reconstruction loss.

On LLaMA and Mistral under aggressive cache compression, CurDKV reports up to 9.6% higher accuracy than methods such as SnapKV and ChunkKV. It also reduces generation latency by up to 40% at high compression and remains compatible with FlashAttention and Grouped Query Attention. These results support selecting retained tokens according to their contribution to the resulting attention output.
neurips-2025-value-guided-kv-compression.tldr: CurDKV uses value-aware matrix decomposition to retain cache entries that preserve attention outputs, improving reported accuracy and latency under strong compression.

paragraphs: Multi-view graph learning combines interconnected information represented through different views. The paper focuses on balancing two useful properties: agreement between views and information that is distinctive to each view. It argues that existing multi-view graph neural networks often do not coordinate these properties effectively.

Multi-view Collaborative Graph Experts, or MvCGE, uses a mixture-of-experts architecture to address that balance. Shared parameters establish consistency across views, while collaborative experts at each layer preserve view-specific information. A graph-aware routing mechanism dynamically activates experts according to the structural characteristics of each view. This makes expert participation responsive to the graph being processed.

Two training objectives reinforce the architecture. A load equilibrium loss is designed to prevent expert collapse and promote balanced specialization, while a graph discrepancy loss based on distributional divergence encourages complementarity between views. Experiments on diverse datasets report superior performance. The findings support coordinating shared representations with structurally informed expert specialization so that the model can use both cross-view agreement and distinctive information.
neurips-2025-where-graph-meets-heterogen.tldr: MvCGE combines shared parameters and dynamically routed graph experts to balance agreement and distinctive information across graph views.
